sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Nantes data is recent, so the trend comes from the Métropole's own figures, and the occupancy figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026. Travel has been shifting away from the car: the share of trips made alone by car fell from 43% in 2015 to 38% in 2025, while cycling rose from 3% to 7% [15]. Public transport carried 154.1 million trips in 2024, above its 2019 level [14]. The regional audit chamber notes that use of the Métropole's public car parks is falling across the board [8].

Nantes has nudged rather than forced. The plan confirmed after a 2023 consultation extends the pedestrian area by 8 hectares to 84 and nearly doubles the limited-traffic zone, phased in through 2024 and 2025 [1]. The low-emission zone that began in 2025 bars only unclassified vehicles, under 1% of the fleet, and only at weekday peak hours [0]. Residents' permits cost €180 a year, with income-based discounts of 30–90% due from April 2023 [2]. Public transport has been free at weekends since April 2021, and so are park-and-ride sites when used with it [4]. On weekdays a park-and-ride ticket costs €4.50 and includes a return trip for up to five people [3].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
Parking has been folded into the transport network. From autumn 2023 buses and trams, bike-share and the NGE and Effia car parks were to share one brand, Naolib [6]. A new app was due in June 2026 to show car park availability and allow bookings and subscriptions alongside transit tickets [13]. The Métropole awarded a concession for six car parks on the west of the centre for 2024–2028, worth about €21.4 million [7]. Street parking has been enforced by number-plate reading since September 2024 [9].

The network keeps adding park-and-ride capacity: Bas-Chantenay and Estuaire opened in early 2025 [12], and Babinière, with 450 spaces on the tram line, in November 2025 [11]. Charging is spreading too: 234 points were already in covered car parks and some park-and-ride sites, and 1,250 public points are being added across the metropolis by 2026 [10]. Tourism is steady, with the summer art trail drawing 4% more visits in 2024 [16].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Two operators run the network's car parks: NGE, the larger with more than 11,000 spaces [8], and Effia. Prices are uniform, €2.30 an hour almost everywhere and €2.70 at a few sites around the hospital, with day tickets of about €22–27, so price says little about which car parks fill.

The 27 car parks average 41% on weekdays and 33% at weekends. The Cathédrale car park is the fullest in the city (86%, as full at weekends), followed by the station's south side (77% and 64%) and the hospital area. The six car parks in the 2024 concession are among the emptiest, averaging 24%, with Les Nefs on the Île de Nantes at 7%. The 20 park-and-ride sites with barriers average only 19% on weekdays and 8% at weekends. A few reach about 50%, while the newest stand almost empty: Babinière at 4%, Bas-Chantenay at 1%.
